stops.title: Walk the mud leg to ring 1
stops.silver: TD does not wait for the end. After every single step it fixes its guess, aiming at the reward it just got plus its own guess for where it landed. You do not have to reach the point to learn you were slow.
stops.do: The game waits at the spawn ring. Walk with WASD to ring 1; leg 1 of the first walk is always mud, so you move at 30% speed. At ring 1 a question floats in front of you: left click for BLUE, right click for ORANGE, melee for both.
stops.predict: Before you click, decide which of the two guesses for the spawn ring could have changed already, when you have walked only one leg of five.
stops.saw: ORANGE's spawn guess already moved, from 15 seconds toward the leg's time plus ORANGE's own guess for ring 1. BLUE is still sitting on 15. Its target is the time from spawn all the way to the point, and you are nowhere near the point yet. One leg in, the split is already there: temporal-difference learning, TD, updates at each step; Monte Carlo waits for the end.
stops.agent: A value model that scores a half-finished conversation can update after every turn. A grader that reads only the final pass or fail has to wait for the last line.

stops.title: Finish the walk and watch BLUE
stops.silver: Driving home, Monte Carlo says nothing the whole trip. Once you arrive, it pulls every forecast you made on the way toward the real arrival time.
stops.do: Leave ring 1 when you are ready and walk to rings 2, 3 and 4 and the point with WASD. Each leg's line turns green for clear or red for mud as you start it. The clock runs only between rings, so you can stand in a ring and read.
stops.predict: Before you leave ring 1, guess which of the ten numbers on the right will change at each ring, and which will all change together at the point.
stops.saw: At each ring one ORANGE number moved: the guess for the ring you had just left. Then, at the point, all five BLUE numbers moved at once, each halfway to the time the rest of that walk really took from its ring. BLUE is Monte Carlo. It learns from real totals, so it had to wait for them. And nobody told either guess how likely mud was.

stops.title: Say which guess leans on a guess
stops.silver: TD moves the forecast made at one landmark toward the forecast made at the next. A guess updated toward a guess, all the way until the arrival grounds the last one in something real.
stops.do: A question floats in front of you. Left click for BLUE, right click for ORANGE.
stops.predict: Lecture 2's Bellman rule says the time from here is this leg plus the time from the next ring; decide which of the two guesses builds its target that way.
stops.saw: ORANGE. Its target is the real time of the leg plus its own current guess for the next ring. Using one of your guesses inside the target of another is called bootstrapping. Lecture 2's rule uses the true time from the next ring, averaged over every way the leg can go. ORANGE has no such thing, so it plugs in one walked leg and a guess.
stops.agent: Training a value model toward its own next-turn predictions is the same move. It can also copy its own errors forward the same way, one turn at a time.

stops.title: Walk again and compare the jumps
stops.silver: Monte Carlo's target is right on average but noisy, because it carries the luck of a whole episode. TD's target leans on its own estimate, so it is biased, but it carries the luck of only one step.
stops.do: Walk the second route from the spawn ring to the point with WASD. The mud is drawn again for every walk, so this one will not match the first.
stops.predict: Before you leave spawn, decide whose spawn guess will jump further on this walk, BLUE's or ORANGE's.
stops.saw: Check how far each spawn number moved on this walk. BLUE's went halfway to this walk's total, mud and all, so one muddy walk drags it a long way. ORANGE's moved toward leg 1 plus its guess for ring 1, and that guess holds news from earlier walks, carried one ring further back each time. Less noise, but only as right as its own guesses. That lean is bias.

stops.title: Bet on which guess swings more
stops.silver: Each target carries a different amount of luck. So the Monte Carlo estimate swings more from episode to episode, and the TD estimate stays steadier but leans on wherever it started.
stops.do: A question floats in front of you: left click for BLUE, right click for ORANGE, melee for about the same. Then walk the third route with WASD.
stops.predict: Commit to whose spawn guess will have moved more in total by the end of the fifth walk.
stops.saw: The total itself comes at stop 7. For now, compare this walk's mud with the walk before. When the amount of mud changes a lot, BLUE's spawn number chases it and ORANGE's barely twitches. The spread a guess picks up from luck is called variance, and here Monte Carlo has more of it.

stops.title: Get cut off at ring 2
stops.silver: TD can learn from a sequence that never finishes, because each update needs only the next step. Monte Carlo needs a complete return from start to end, or it has nothing to learn from.
stops.do: A question floats in front of you: left click for BLUE, right click for ORANGE, melee for neither. Then walk the fourth route with WASD; at ring 2 the round ends and the walk stops there.
stops.predict: Commit to which guesses will learn anything from a walk that never reaches the point.
stops.saw: ORANGE changed its guesses for spawn and ring 1, one for each leg you walked. BLUE changed nothing. No arrival, no total, nothing to move toward. The fight ended before you got there, and only the guess that updates at every corner got anything out of the walk.
stops.agent: An agent run that times out halfway still trains a TD-style value model. A pass-or-fail grader gets nothing from it at all.

stops.title: Ask what a planner would need
stops.silver: Lecture 3's planner, dynamic programming, bootstraps without sampling: it is handed the rules and averages over every outcome. Monte Carlo samples without bootstrapping. TD does both.
stops.do: A question floats in front of you: left click for only the map, right click for each leg's mud odds and speeds, melee for nothing more. Then walk the fifth and last route with WASD.
stops.predict: Lecture 3's planner filled in values without walking at all; decide what it would need to be told to do that here.
stops.saw: It would need the rules: how likely mud is on each leg, and how slow it makes you. Neither BLUE nor ORANGE was told any of that. Both learned from walks alone, which is model-free prediction. At the point, the coach line gives how far each spawn guess moved in total over the five walks. BLUE's total is usually the larger one.

stops.title: Read what the walks showed
stops.silver: Between one-step TD and Monte Carlo sit n-step returns: a few real steps, then a guess. Lambda blends them all. The two guesses you just watched are the two ends of one dial.
stops.do: Nothing to press. Read the three lines on the left and your prediction score; then the game ends.
stops.predict: Before you read, say in one sentence which guess you would trust after five walks, and which after five hundred.
stops.saw: BLUE, Monte Carlo, used real totals: no bias, more noise, and nothing from the cut walk. ORANGE, TD, used one leg plus its own guess: steadier, bent by its guesses, and learning before the end. One honest warning: five walks with a fixed half step are far too few for either to settle. Treat the numbers as a demonstration, not a result.
stops.agent: Judge each turn of an agent by the final score and you are doing Monte Carlo. Judge it by how a value model's estimate moved across that turn and you are doing TD.
